Q: PyTorch training issue with EfficientNetB3 | Validation Accuracy plateu A:

Are gradients flowing through the implementation? Roughly looking at your implementation is that the logits stuff is wrapped in no grad which maybe a problem. Checkout this resnet implementation (https://github.com/ronghuaiyang/arcface-pytorch/tree/master/models).

Also probably remove label smoothing with ArcFace and also check if any logits are NaN

Is your res still 128 x 128?

Q: How can I guarantee the fingerprint value was not faked in the request from client side? A:

Checking the integrity of client side fingerprint is not possible.... The best bet for you is to use PHP to detect the internal systems... I wrote a library to that but not published... If you need it I can send it to you...

What this library does is to detect the Mac address of the device... Since two system can't have same Mac address... It's a very good way of getting accurate fingerprint.

Q: Label factor levels from a lookup table (using labelled package) A:

Up front, I'm not a labelled-guru, but on reading https://larmarange.github.io/labelled/articles/labelled.html#value-labels, one way is to apply labelled() to each column of dummy_dat with the applicable element of dic_test.

for (nm in names(dummy_dat)) dummy_dat[[nm]] <- labelled(dummy_dat[[nm]], dic_test[[nm]])
dummy_dat
#   X1 X2_1 X2_2 X3
# 1  1    1    3  1
# 2  2    2    2  2
# 3  1    3    1  3
dummy_dat$X2_1
# <labelled<double>[3]>
# [1] 1 2 3
# Labels:
#  value     label
#      1     never
#      2 sometimes
#      3    always

If you are interested in using dplyr/tidyr and/or are using them elsewhere, your data path can be redone like this:

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(labelled)
dic_test <- pivot_longer(dummy_labels, cols = -question) |>
  mutate(name = gsub("x", "", name)) |>
  dictionary_to_value_labels(names_from = question, values_from = name, labels_from = value, data = dummy_dat)
dummy_dat2 <- dummy_dat |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ labelled(.x, dic_test[[cur_column()]])))
dummy_dat2
#   X1 X2_1 X2_2 X3
# 1  1    1    3  1
# 2  2    2    2  2
# 3  1    3    1  3
dummy_dat2$X2_2
# <labelled<double>[3]>
# [1] 3 2 1
# Labels:
#  value     label
#      1     never
#      2 sometimes
#      3    always

Q: Why there are empty spaces in the middle of the string returned by re.split()? A:

Note the original Question you reference is about str.split(), not re.split() - while the usage is often similar, I highly doubt there's any designed intention to complement str.join() too and there's also no re.join()!

As for why, this is actually described in the re.split() docs

If there are capturing groups in the separator and it matches at the start of the string, the result will start with an empty string. The same holds for the end of the string

>>> re.split(r"(\s)", "Hello! How are you?")
['Hello!', ' ', 'How', ' ', 'are', ' ', 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"\s", "Hello! How are you?")
['Hello!', 'How', 'are', 'you?']

Combined with @STerliakov's comment, we have a good explanation: using a capture group which matches a block will begin an empty string, then matching again leads to keeping this empty string

This Answer to How to group a regular expression in re.split() function? provides further insight, you can use a non-capturing group to skip these values in the results too

With a simpler string

>>> re.split(r"[12]", "0123")      # split on match, hole for successive
['0', '', '3']
>>> re.split(r"([12])", "0123")    # capture group keeps matches in result
['0', '1', '', '2', '3']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[12])", "0123")  # non-capturing group maintains hole
['0', '', '3']

So N matches leads to N-1 holes

>>> re.split(r"(?:[123])", "01234")
['0', '', '', '4']
>>> re.split(r"([123])", "01234")
['0', '1', '', '2', '', '3', '4']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[123456789])", "0123456789")
['0', '', '', '', '', '', '', '', '', '']

Combined with the quick duplicate marking (which suggests + to combine the successive matches), we can make make something a little nicer, with some choices dependent on if you want that ! and/or ? in the same result tokens

>>> re.split(r"(?:[12345678])", "0123456789")
['0', '', '', '', '', '', '', '', '9']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[12345678])+", "0123456789")
['0', '9']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[123456789])+", "0123456789")  # unfortunately has trailing
['0', '']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[123456789]+)", "0123456789")  # when ending matches too
['0', '']

>>> re.split(r"(!|\s)", "Hello! How are you?")     # switch to OR
['Hello', '!', '', ' ', 'How', ' ', 'are', ' ', 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"(!|\s)+", "Hello! How are you?")    # OR with +
['Hello', ' ', 'How', ' ', 'are', ' ', 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"((!)|\s)+", "Hello! How are you?")  # another capture group
['Hello', ' ', '!', 'How', ' ', None, 'are', ' ', None, 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"(?:(!)|\s)+", "Hello! How are you?")  # non-capture outer
['Hello', '!', 'How', None, 'are', None, 'you?']

Finally, you can always use filter(None, my_iterable) to drop Falsey values from some iterable and may also find re.findall() or re.finditer() is a better fit, though this steps around the explanation

>>> re.findall(r"\w+", "Hello! How are you?")       # "words"
['Hello', 'How', 'are', 'you']
>>> re.findall(r"[\w\?!]+", "Hello! How are you?")  # words and also ?,!
['Hello!', 'How', 'are', 'you?']
>>> re.findall(r"\w+|\?", "Hello! How are you?")    # ? is its own token
['Hello', 'How', 'are', 'you', '?']

Q: Is there any smart way to get rid of the empty strings returned by re.split() in python? A:

Besides the already mentioned +, you can force empty strings at start and end and then unconditionally slice them away:

re.split('[().]+', f'({x})')[1:-1]

Q: How can I get vscode recent file/folder/workspaces on linux with cli tools or via code? A:

For cli, you could do something like this: sqlite3 $HOME/.config/Code/User/globalStorage/state.vscdb "select value from ItemTable where key='history.recentlyOpenedPathsList';" | jq .entries. The keys of the objects in the array would be like folderUri or fileUri depending on the type of what was opened.
